title: How the work grows
concept: Searching · counting steps as lists grow
description: Compare the two searches by counting, not timing: how many looks does each need as the archive grows?

tasks.title: Count the steps, not the seconds
tasks.body:
How long a program takes depends on the computer, so computer scientists count steps instead.

The question is how the steps grow as the input grows: a linear search of n items needs up to n looks, a binary search only as many as the times n can be halved.
tasks.detail: Halving: 8 items halve to 4, 2, 1, 0, which is four halvings, so a binary search of 8 needs at most 4 looks. Doubling the list adds only one more look. That gap is why sorted data is worth the effort of sorting.

tasks.code:
# How many halvings until nothing is left?
for size in [1, 2, 7, 8, 1000]:
    n = size
    halvings = 0
    while n > 0:
        n = n // 2
        halvings = halvings + 1
    print(size, halvings)
tasks.note: 1,000 items need only 10 halvings. Going from 7 items to 8 adds one, because 8 is a power of two.

tasks.question: A list grows from 1,000 items to 2,000. How many more looks can a binary search need, at most?
tasks.why: Doubling the list adds one halving.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: add 1,000,000 to the sizes and guess its halvings first. Then add a column with the linear worst case, the size itself.

Write three functions that count the looks a search needs.

1. linear_worst(n) returns the most looks a linear search needs for a list of n items.
2. binary_worst(n) returns the most looks a binary search needs, which is how many times n can be halved with // 2 before it reaches 0 (0 for an empty list).
3. compare(sizes) takes a list of sizes and returns a list of [size, linear, binary] lists, one per size, in the same order.

Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: The linear worst case is simply every item. For the binary one, count halvings in a loop: n = n // 2, adding one each time, while n is more than 0.
compare() builds a list: for each size, a list of the size and the two counts, worked out by calling the other two functions.
With other names: doublings = 0, then while value < limit: value = value * 2 and doublings = doublings + 1.

error_hints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, and call the other functions by their names.
compare() returns a list of lists: append [size, linear, binary] for each size.
binary_worst(0) should return 0: an empty list needs no looks.
Check an odd size just below a power of two.

similar_example.code:
value = 1
doublings = 0
while value < 1000:
    value = value * 2
    doublings = doublings + 1
print(doublings)
similar_example.note: Counting doublings up to 1,000 rather than halvings down from it. The two counts match, which is the heart of binary search.

other_ways.note: bit_length() is how many bits n needs in binary, which is exactly how many times it can be halved. Unit 1 and unit 3 meet.
log2() counts halvings with a formula. It is the "log n" you will meet in books about algorithms.

cases.description: a size just below a power of two
